# Book I, Proposition 17

*Two angles of a triangle are less than two right angles*

> In any triangle two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/17-idea.svg" alt="Put any two angles of a triangle side by side (blue and yellow), and they always fall short of a straight line, which makes two right angles." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Put any two angles of a triangle side by side (blue and yellow), and they always fall short of a straight line, which makes two right angles.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/17.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.17, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ABC be a triangle;

I say that two angles of the triangle ABC taken together in any manner are less than two right angles.

For let BC be produced to D. [Post. 2]

Then, since the angle ACD is an exterior angle of the triangle ABC,

it is greater than the interior and opposite angle ABC. [I. 16]

Let the angle ACB be added to each;

therefore the angles ACD, ACB are greater than the angles ABC, BCA.

But the angles ACD, ACB are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]

Therefore the angles ABC, BCA are less than two right angles.

Similarly we can prove that the angles BAC, ACB are also less than two right angles, and so are the angles CAB, ABC as well.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop17.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop17.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- In any triangle two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles. -/
theorem Prop17 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) :
    ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟ ∧ ∠ B A C + ∠ A C B < ∟ + ∟ ∧ ∠ C A B + ∠ A B C < ∟ + ∟ := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle;
  -- I say that two angles of the triangle ABC taken together in any manner are less than two
  -- right angles.
  /- "In any manner": any two of the three angles, so three sums. Euclid's argument is
     for the angles ABC, BCA; we give it for every triangle, in his letters, and use
     it for each pair below. -/
  have less : ∀ {A B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟ := by
    intro A B C hABC
    have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
    have hB_C : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
    have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
    -- For let BC be produced to D. [Post. 2]
    obtain ⟨BC, hB_BC, hC_BC⟩ := Postulate1 B C hB_C
    obtain ⟨D, hD_BC, hBCD, -⟩ := Postulate2 hB_BC hC_BC hB_C []
    -- Then, since the angle ACD is an exterior angle of the triangle ABC,
    -- it is greater than the interior and opposite angle ABC. [I. 16]
    /- I.16 names the interior angle from C, as CBA; it is the angle ABC read the
       other way round (`angle_symm`). -/
    have hABC_ACD : ∠ A B C < ∠ A C D := by
      rw [angle_symm hA_B hB_C.symm]
      exact (Prop16 hABC hBCD).1
    -- Let the angle ACB be added to each;
    /- The same angle added to a greater and a less leaves the first sum greater: no
       Common Notion says so, but a tacit law of magnitudes does (`add_lt_add_right`,
       System E §3.5). -/
    have hadded : ∠ A B C + ∠ A C B < ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B := add_lt_add_right (∠ A C B) hABC_ACD
    -- therefore the angles ACD, ACB are greater than the angles ABC, BCA.
    /- The angle ACB, added to ABC, is the angle BCA read the other way round. -/
    have hgreater : ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B := by
      rw [angle_symm hB_C hA_C]
      exact hadded
    -- But the angles ACD, ACB are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]
    /- AC stands on BD, which is BC produced; A is off it, since ABC is a triangle
       (`Triangle.off_line`, `Triangle.of_line`). I.13 names the two angles BCA, ACD. -/
    have hA_BC : ¬ OnLine A BC := hABC.bca.off_line hB_BC hC_BC
    have hBDA : Triangle B D A := Triangle.of_line hB_BC hD_BC (ne_of_between_ends hBCD) hA_BC
    have htwo : ∠ A C D + ∠ A C B = ∟ + ∟ := by
      rw [add_comm (∠ A C D), angle_symm hA_C hB_C]
      exact Prop13 hBCD hBDA
    -- Therefore the angles ABC, BCA are less than two right angles.
    rw [← htwo]
    exact hgreater
  /- Euclid's own figure: the angles ABC, BCA. -/
  have hABC_BCA : ∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟ := less hABC
  -- Similarly we can prove that the angles BAC, ACB are also less than two right angles, and
  -- so are the angles CAB, ABC as well.
  /- The same argument in the triangle BAC: AC is produced, and the exterior angle at C
     is greater than the angle BAC. And in the triangle CAB: AB is produced, and the
     exterior angle at B is greater than the angle CAB. -/
  have hBAC_ACB : ∠ B A C + ∠ A C B < ∟ + ∟ := less hABC.bac
  have hCAB_ABC : ∠ C A B + ∠ A B C < ∟ + ∟ := less hABC.cab
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hABC_BCA, hBAC_ACB, hCAB_ABC⟩
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**Any two.** "Taken together in any manner" is, Heath notes, "πάντῃ μεταλαμβανόμεναι, i.e. any pair added together" (vol. 1, p. 282). So the Lean statement says three things, in Euclid's letters: the angles ABC, BCA; the angles BAC, ACB; and the angles CAB, ABC. Euclid argues for the first pair and says "similarly" for the others. As in I.16, the Lean gives his argument once, for every triangle, and uses it three times, producing BC, AC and AB in turn.

**Equals added to unequals.** "Let the angle ACB be added to each" carries no citation, and no Common Notion fits: the second adds equals to equals. The manuscripts and editions add others, among them "If equals be added to unequals, the wholes are unequal", which Heiberg prints in brackets and Heath rejects: "(a) stands self-condemned because 'unequal' tells us nothing. It is easy to see what is wanted if we refer to I. 17, where the same angle is added to a *greater* and a *less*, and it is inferred that the first sum is greater than the second" (vol. 1, p. 223). What is wanted is the tacit law of magnitudes `add_lt_add_right` (System E §3.5): adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". Our Common Notions 3 and 5 are proved from it, and here it is cited on its own.

**The converse is a postulate.** Postulate 5 is the converse of I.17, and Proclus held that against it: "This ought even to be struck out of the Postulates altogether; for it is a theorem involving many difficulties … And the converse of it is actually proved by Euclid himself as a theorem" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 202). In Lean, Postulate 5 assumes `∠ A B C + ∠ B C D < ∟ + ∟` and concludes that the straight lines meet, while I.17 starts from a triangle and concludes `∠ A B C + ∠ B C A < ∟ + ∟`. I.17 needs no Postulate 5 and holds in the geometry of János Bolyai and Nikolai Lobachevsky too, but not in Bernhard Riemann's (see I.16), where a triangle with a corner at the pole of a straight line and the other two on it has two right angles.

**The modern way.** Put B at 0, C at 1 and A at a, above them, in the complex plane: the angle ABC is arg a, and the angle BCA is π − arg(a − 1). Since a − 1 lies straight to the left of a, its argument is the larger, so the two angles together fall short of π by arg(a − 1) − arg a. That shortfall is the angle BAC, but saying so is I.32, which needs the parallel postulate.
